claims.notes: The general rule that the subsection (d) exemptions cut into. Subsection (c) (the 1982 window-period loans) was read and is not described on the page. Must be stated with im-garn-exempt-transfers-on-death.

claims.claim: Under 12 U.S.C. 1701j-3(d), for a real property loan secured by a lien on residential real property containing less than five dwelling units, a lender may not exercise its option under a due-on-sale clause upon a transfer by devise, descent, or operation of law on the death of a joint tenant or tenant by the entirety, upon a transfer to a relative resulting from the death of a borrower, or upon a transfer where the spouse or children of the borrower become an owner of the property.
claims.quotedLanguage: With respect to a real property loan secured by a lien on residential real property containing less than five dwelling units, including a lien on the stock allocated to a dwelling unit in a cooperative housing corporation, or on a residential manufactured home, a lender may not exercise its option pursuant to a due-on-sale clause upon ... (3) a transfer by devise, descent, or operation of law on the death of a joint tenant or tenant by the entirety; ... (5) a transfer to a relative resulting from the death of a borrower; ... (6) a transfer where the spouse or children of the borrower become an owner of the property;
claims.notes: TRAPS. (1) The section does not define 'relative'. Do not say who qualifies; an heir who is not a relative, an LLC or a non-family devisee is a question for an attorney. (2) 'less than five dwelling units': quote it, do not round it to 'homes'. (3) The exemption stops the lender from calling the loan due BECAUSE OF THE TRANSFER. It says nothing about missed payments; the loan can still be foreclosed for default. Never write that the lender 'cannot foreclose' on an inherited house. (4) It does not make the heir the borrower, and it does not require the lender to approve an assumption. (5) Paragraphs (1), (2), (4), (7), (8) and (9) of subsection (d) are other exemptions not used on the page. (6) Subsection (e)(2) lets regulations permit exercise of the clause for loans tied to 'the right to receive future income' (reverse-mortgage type agreements); the page is about ordinary mortgages only.

claims.claim: 12 U.S.C. 1701j-3(b)(3) says that, in exercising its option under a due-on-sale clause, a lender is encouraged to permit an assumption of the loan at the existing contract rate or at a rate at or below the average between the contract and market rates, and that nothing in the section prohibits such an assumption.
claims.quotedLanguage: In the exercise of its option under a due-on-sale clause, a lender is encouraged to permit an assumption of a real property loan at the existing contract rate or at a rate which is at or below the average between the contract and market rates, and nothing in this section shall be interpreted to prohibit any such assumption.
claims.notes: 'Encouraged' is not 'required'. The statute gives no right to assume a loan. MEDIUM because the sentence sits in the general rule about a lender exercising the clause, not in the death-transfer exemption; the page must present it only as encouragement and must not say a lender has to allow an assumption or keep the rate.

claims.claim: Regulation X, 12 CFR 1024.31, defines a successor in interest as a person to whom an ownership interest in a property securing a covered mortgage loan is transferred from a borrower, where the transfer is one of five listed kinds, including a transfer by devise, descent, or operation of law on the death of a joint tenant or tenant by the entirety, a transfer to a relative resulting from the death of a borrower, and a transfer where the spouse or children of the borrower become an owner of the property.
claims.quotedLanguage: Successor in interest means a person to whom an ownership interest in a property securing a mortgage loan subject to this subpart is transferred from a borrower, provided that the transfer is: ... A transfer by devise, descent, or operation of law on the death of a joint tenant or tenant by the entirety; ... A transfer to a relative resulting from the death of a borrower; ... A transfer where the spouse or children of the borrower become an owner of the property;
claims.notes: The list mirrors five of the due-on-sale exemptions in 12 U.S.C. 1701j-3(d). The other two listed transfers (divorce decree, inter vivos trust) are not used on the page. 'Mortgage loan subject to this subpart' means a federally related mortgage loan and excludes open-end home equity lines (same section); the page does not describe HELOCs. TRAP: Idaho Code 45-1506 also uses the words 'successor in interest' for a different purpose; do not treat the two as one definition.

claims.claim: 12 CFR 1024.31 defines a confirmed successor in interest as a successor in interest once a servicer has confirmed that person's identity and ownership interest in a property that secures a covered mortgage loan.
claims.quotedLanguage: Confirmed successor in interest means a successor in interest once a servicer has confirmed the successor in interest's identity and ownership interest in a property that secures a mortgage loan subject to this subpart.
claims.notes: Confirmation is the servicer's act. The regulation sets no number of days for it (see im-regx-servicer-policies-after-death: 'promptly').

claims.claim: Under 12 CFR 1024.30(d), a confirmed successor in interest is considered a borrower for purposes of 12 CFR 1024.17 and the mortgage servicing subpart of Regulation X.
claims.quotedLanguage: Successors in interest. A confirmed successor in interest shall be considered a borrower for purposes of § 1024.17 and this subpart.
claims.notes: TRAP: 'borrower' here is a status under the federal servicing rules (information, notices, error resolution, loss mitigation procedures). It does not make the person liable on the note: see im-regx-successor-not-liable-unless-assumes. State with af-regx-scope: small servicers are outside 1024.38 through 1024.41, and 1024.39 through 1024.41 reach only a loan secured by the borrower's principal residence. 1024.17 (escrow accounts) was not read.

claims.claim: Under 12 CFR 1024.36(i)(1), when a person sends a written request indicating that the person may be a successor in interest, with the name of the borrower from whom the person received an ownership interest and information identifying the loan account, the servicer must respond with a written description of the documents it reasonably requires to confirm the person's identity and ownership interest in the property, and with contact information, including a telephone number, for further assistance.
claims.quotedLanguage: With respect to any written request from a person that indicates that the person may be a successor in interest and that includes the name of the transferor borrower from whom the person received an ownership interest and information that enables the servicer to identify the mortgage loan account, a servicer shall respond by providing the potential successor in interest with a written description of the documents the servicer reasonably requires to confirm the person's identity and ownership interest in the property and contact information, including a telephone number, for further assistance.
claims.notes: The request must be WRITTEN. Paragraph (i)(4): if the servicer has established an address for information requests, it need only comply for requests received at that address. Paragraph (i)(1) applies paragraphs (c) through (g) (acknowledgment and response time limits) to the request; those paragraphs are in the cached page but were NOT turned into claims, so the page gives no day count for the servicer's reply.

claims.claim: Under 12 CFR 1024.36(i)(3), before confirmation a servicer responding to such a request is not required to provide any information other than the description of required documents and contact information, and if the request asks for other information the servicer must indicate that the potential successor in interest may resubmit the request once confirmed.
claims.quotedLanguage: In responding to a request under paragraph (i)(1) of this section prior to confirmation, the servicer is not required to provide any information other than the information specified in paragraphs (i)(1) and (2) of this section. In responding to a written request under paragraph (i)(1) that requests other information, the servicer must indicate that the potential successor in interest may resubmit any request for information once confirmed as a successor in interest.
claims.notes: This is why an heir may be refused balance or payment history until ownership is documented. Do not describe this as the servicer acting wrongly.

claims.claim: 12 CFR 1024.38(b)(1)(vi) requires a servicer's policies and procedures to be reasonably designed to ensure that, on notice of a borrower's death, it can promptly facilitate communication with potential or confirmed successors in interest; on notice of a potential successor, promptly determine and describe the documents it reasonably requires to confirm identity and ownership interest; and on receipt of those documents, promptly make a confirmation determination and notify the person that it has confirmed the person's status, needs additional documents, or has determined the person is not a successor in interest.
claims.quotedLanguage: Upon receiving notice of the death of a borrower or of any transfer of the property securing a mortgage loan, promptly facilitate communication with any potential or confirmed successors in interest regarding the property; ... Upon receiving notice of the existence of a potential successor in interest, promptly determine the documents the servicer reasonably requires to confirm that person's identity and ownership interest in the property and promptly provide to the potential successor in interest a description of those documents and how the person may submit a written request under § 1024.36(i) (including the appropriate address); and ... Upon the receipt of such documents, promptly make a confirmation determination and promptly notify the person, as applicable, that the servicer has confirmed the person's status, has determined that additional documents are required (and what those documents are), or has determined that the person is not a successor in interest.
claims.notes: TRAPS. (1) This is a policies-and-procedures objective ('reasonably designed to ensure that the servicer can'), not a per-loan deadline; the word is 'promptly' and there is no day count. (2) Under 1024.30(b) small servicers, reverse mortgages and certain qualified lenders are outside 1024.38 (existing claim af-regx-scope); always carry that limit. (3) Whether a private person can sue over 1024.38 was not researched; say nothing about remedies.

claims.claim: 12 CFR 1024.32(c)(1) lets a servicer send a confirmed successor in interest who is not liable on the loan a written notice, which must explain that unless the successor assumes the mortgage loan obligation under State law, the successor is not liable for the mortgage debt and cannot be required to use the successor's assets to pay it, except that the lender has a security interest in the property and a right to foreclose on the property when permitted by law and authorized under the mortgage loan contract.
claims.quotedLanguage: Unless the successor in interest assumes the mortgage loan obligation under State law, the successor in interest is not liable for the mortgage debt and cannot be required to use the successor in interest's assets to pay the mortgage debt, except that the lender has a security interest in the property and a right to foreclose on the property, when permitted by law and authorized under the mortgage loan contract;
claims.notes: TRAPS. (1) The quoted words are the required CONTENT OF AN OPTIONAL NOTICE ('a servicer may provide'), addressed to a successor 'who is not liable on the mortgage loan obligation'. They are not a freestanding rule that no heir is ever liable. A co-borrower, a co-signer, a surviving spouse who signed the note, or someone who assumes the loan is in a different position, and Idaho community-property and estate-claims rules were NOT researched. Attribute and point to an attorney. (2) Always carry the second half: the lender keeps its lien and its right to foreclose. (3) What counts as assuming a loan 'under State law' in Idaho was not researched.

claims.claim: Under 12 CFR 1024.32(c), the optional notice comes with an acknowledgment form; the notice must say there is no time limit to return it but that the servicer will not begin sending certain notices and communications until it is returned, and a servicer that sent the notice need not provide specified written disclosures to the confirmed successor until the successor either assumes the loan under State law or returns the acknowledgment.
claims.quotedLanguage: Informs the successor in interest that there is no time limit to return the acknowledgment but that the servicer will not begin sending such notices and communications to the confirmed successor in interest until the acknowledgment is returned; ... until the confirmed successor in interest either assumes the mortgage loan obligation under State law or executes an acknowledgment that complies with paragraph (c)(1)(iv) of this section and provides it to the servicer.
claims.notes: The acknowledgment form states that the notices 'do not make the successor in interest liable for the mortgage debt' (paragraph (c)(1)(iv)(B), read, not separately claimed). Under (c)(4) a servicer also need not send a confirmed successor disclosures it is already sending to another borrower on the account. Do not tell a reader to sign or not sign anything.

claims.claim: Under 12 CFR 1024.32(c)(1)(v), the notice must also explain that whether or not the successor in interest signs the acknowledgment, the successor is entitled to submit notices of error under 12 CFR 1024.35, requests for information under 12 CFR 1024.36, and requests for a payoff statement under 12 CFR 1026.36 for the mortgage loan account.
claims.quotedLanguage: Whether or not the successor in interest executes the acknowledgment described in paragraph (c)(1)(iv) of this section, the successor in interest is entitled to submit notices of error under § 1024.35, requests for information under § 1024.36, and requests for a payoff statement under § 1026.36 with respect to the mortgage loan account, with a brief explanation of those rights and how to exercise them, including appropriate address information.
claims.notes: Applies to a CONFIRMED successor in interest (the notice is sent 'upon confirmation'). 12 CFR 1026.36(c)(3) and 1026.2(a)(11) (Regulation Z) were not read for this page; give no day count for a payoff statement. Pair with existing af-cfpb-payoff-amount for what a payoff amount is.

claims.claim: The CFPB says a person who has inherited a home should inform the loan servicer, and that to receive certain information about the mortgage account the person may need to show the servicer proof of their right to the home, which after a death might include a copy of the executed will and the death certificate or a letter from the executor of the estate; the servicer should say what proof it needs, and the proof available may vary from state to state. The page describes the mortgage servicer as the company that sends the monthly mortgage statement, responds to borrower inquiries and keeps track of principal and interest paid.
claims.quotedLanguage: To receive certain information about the mortgage account, you may need to show the mortgage servicer proof of your right to the home. In the case of inheritance from someone who has died, that proof might include a copy of the executed will and the death certificate or a letter from the executor of the deceased person's estate. The mortgage servicer should tell you what kind of proof it needs. The proof that you can get may vary from state to state. ... The mortgage servicer is the company that sends the monthly mortgage statement, responds to borrower inquiries and keeps track of principal and interest paid.
claims.notes: Consumer guidance, 'last reviewed' Sep 11, 2024. The CFPB's examples ('might include') are not a list of what an Idaho servicer will accept. Idaho calls the executor a personal representative (existing claim pb-letters-required); the CFPB's word is 'executor'.

claims.claim: The CFPB suggests asking the servicer about rights and obligations with respect to the house and the mortgage, for example how to continue making payments on the loan or how to seek a loan modification, and says the person may also want to consult an attorney or a housing counselor, and may need an attorney if facing imminent foreclosure or served with legal papers.
claims.quotedLanguage: You also may want to ask the servicer for further information about your rights and obligations with respect to the house and the mortgage. For example, you might ask the servicer how you can continue making payments on the loan or how you can seek a loan modification. ... If you're facing imminent foreclosure or have been served with legal papers, you may also need to consult an attorney
claims.notes: Guidance, not a rule. A modification is something to ask about, never something promised.

claims.claim: In a December 2024 issue spotlight, the CFPB wrote that people who become homeowners after the death of a spouse or family member, where there is a mortgage on the home, must act quickly to make mortgage payments in order to avoid foreclosure, and that the homeowner may in some circumstances wish to assume liability for the mortgage.
claims.quotedLanguage: If there is a mortgage on the home, these homeowners must act quickly to make mortgage payments in order to avoid foreclosure. And the homeowner may in some circumstances wish to assume liability for the mortgage.
claims.notes: A CFPB research publication dated DEC 17, 2024, not a regulation. MEDIUM: it is an agency report from a prior CFPB leadership period and could be withdrawn or archived; re-open the URL before each refresh. Used as the attributed basis for 'payments still fall due'. Do not turn 'must act quickly' into a deadline.

claims.claim: The same CFPB spotlight says federal rules and mortgage program guidelines require servicers to help successor homeowners get the information they need to manage the existing mortgage and, if the homeowner chooses, to assume the existing loan terms, and reports that homeowners describe being incorrectly told that they must refinance the loan at higher interest rates rather than being offered options for managing the existing mortgage.
claims.quotedLanguage: Federal rules and mortgage program guidelines require servicers to help these successor homeowners get the information they need to manage the existing mortgage and, if the homeowner chooses, to assume the existing loan terms. ... Homeowners report being incorrectly told that they must refinance the loan at today's higher interest rates, rather than being offered options for managing the existing mortgage.
claims.notes: TRAPS. (1) The second sentence reports COMPLAINTS ('Homeowners report'); it is not a finding against any servicer and not a statement that refinancing is never required. (2) 'mortgage program guidelines' refers to investor and federal program rules (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA, VA, USDA) that were NOT read; whether a given loan is assumable depends on the loan and its investor. Do not write that an heir has a right to assume. (3) 'today's higher interest rates' is a December 2024 statement; do not repeat it as a current fact about rates.

claims.claim: In a 2014 interpretive rule published in the Federal Register, the CFPB described a successor as a person who receives legal interest in a property, typically by a transfer from a family member, by operation of law upon another's death, or under a divorce decree or separation agreement, and stated that where the successor acquires property that is subject to a mortgage, the successor is not personally liable for the associated debt but may choose to assume the debt.
claims.quotedLanguage: A successor is a person who receives legal interest in a property, typically by a transfer from a family member, by operation of law upon another's death, or under a divorce decree or separation agreement. ... In all of these situations, where the successor acquires property that is subject to a mortgage, the successor is not personally liable for the associated debt, but may choose to assume the debt.
claims.notes: 79 FR 41631 (July 17, 2014), document 2014-16780. The sentence is the Bureau's background description in an interpretive rule about Regulation Z, not a holding about Idaho law. Same caveats as im-regx-successor-not-liable-unless-assumes: a person who also signed the note, and Idaho community-property or estate-claims questions, are outside it. MEDIUM because the document is from 2014 and its current status in Regulation Z's official interpretations was not checked.

claims.claim: The CFPB's 2014 interpretive rule states that where a successor who has previously acquired title to a dwelling agrees to be added as obligor or substituted for the existing obligor on the loan secured by that dwelling, and that addition or substitution is not an 'assumption' as Regulation Z defines the term, it is not subject to the Ability-to-Repay Rule's requirements; it adds that even where a due-on-sale clause may be exercised, creditors may agree to add the successor as a named obligor under the loan contract.
claims.quotedLanguage: The Bureau has been asked whether the creditor is obligated under the ATR Rule to determine the successor's ability to repay the mortgage before formally adding the successor as an obligor. ... such addition or substitution is not subject to the ATR Rule's requirements. A creditor may rely on this interpretation as a safe harbor under section 130(f) of TILA. ... Even where a due-on-sale clause may be exercised, however, creditors may agree to add the successor as a named obligor under the loan contract.
claims.notes: TRAPS. (1) This removes a FEDERAL requirement (the ability-to-repay determination) from that step. It does not stop a creditor or investor from applying its own underwriting, and it does not oblige a creditor to add anyone: the text says creditors 'may agree'. (2) Issued 2014 ('effective July 17, 2014 and applicable beginning July 8, 2014'). The Bureau said it planned to move the interpretation into Regulation Z's official interpretations; whether and how that was done, and whether it has changed since, was NOT checked. The page dates the statement to 2014. (3) The rule distinguishes a consumer WITHOUT an existing interest who takes over a loan to buy a home: that is an assumption and is subject to ability-to-repay. A buyer taking over an heir's loan is in that second group.

claims.claim: Idaho Code 15-2-609 provides that a specific devise passes subject to any security interest existing at the date of death, without right of exoneration, regardless of a general directive in the will to pay debts.
claims.quotedLanguage: A specific devise passes subject to any security interest existing at the date of death, without right of exoneration, regardless of a general directive in the will to pay debts.
claims.notes: TRAPS. (1) The section speaks of a SPECIFIC DEVISE (a gift of particular property by will). It does not address a house passing by intestacy, a residuary gift, a will that specifically directs the mortgage to be paid, community property, or property passing outside probate. Do not generalise it to 'heirs always take the house with the mortgage'. (2) 'Specific devise' and 'security interest' are not defined in this section; definitions elsewhere in Title 15 were not read. (3) Explain 'exoneration' only as the statute uses it: the devise passes subject to the security interest even if the will has a general direction to pay debts. Future-dated check: an existing registry note (pb-letters-required, 2026-11-12) records that the 2026 session's one PROBATE bill, S1240 (Ch. 79, effective 01/01/2027), replaces chapter 5 and amends 15-1-201 only; this section is not among them. That note was relied on, not re-run. The section page showed no effective-date banner on 2026-11-13.

claims.claim: Under Idaho Code 15-3-814, if any assets of an estate are encumbered by a mortgage, pledge, lien or other security interest, the personal representative may pay the encumbrance or any part of it, renew or extend the secured obligation, or convey or transfer the assets to the creditor in satisfaction of the lien, in whole or in part, whether or not the holder has presented a claim, if it appears to be for the best interest of the estate; payment of an encumbrance does not increase the share of the distributee entitled to the encumbered assets unless the distributee is entitled to exoneration.
claims.quotedLanguage: If any assets of the estate are encumbered by mortgage, pledge, lien, or other security interest, the personal representative may pay the encumbrance or any part thereof, renew or extend any obligation secured by the encumbrance or convey or transfer the assets to the creditor in satisfaction of his lien, in whole or in part, whether or not the holder of the encumbrance has presented a claim, if it appears to be for the best interest of the estate. Payment of an encumbrance does not increase the share of the distributee entitled to the encumbered assets unless the distributee is entitled to exoneration.
claims.notes: Permissive ('may') and conditioned on 'the best interest of the estate'. It is a power of an APPOINTED personal representative (existing claim pb-letters-required), not of an heir acting alone. It does not say the estate MUST keep the mortgage current. A transfer to the creditor needs the creditor to accept it; the section does not oblige a lender to take the property. State with existing id-pr-powers-limited-by-will where the page talks about a personal representative's powers generally. Future-dated check: an existing registry note (pb-letters-required, 2026-11-12) records that the 2026 session's one PROBATE bill, S1240 (Ch. 79, effective 01/01/2027), replaces chapter 5 and amends 15-1-201 only; this section is not among them. That note was relied on, not re-run. The section page showed no effective-date banner on 2026-11-13.

claims.claim: Idaho Code 15-3-812 bars execution or levy against estate property under a judgment against a decedent or a personal representative, and states that the section shall not be construed to prevent the enforcement of mortgages, pledges or liens upon real or personal property in an appropriate proceeding.
claims.quotedLanguage: No execution may issue upon nor may any levy be made against any property of the estate under any judgment against a decedent or a personal representative, but this section shall not be construed to prevent the enforcement of mortgages, pledges or liens upon real or personal property in an appropriate proceeding.
claims.notes: The statute says 'mortgages, pledges or liens'; it does not use the words 'deed of trust' or 'trustee's sale'. The page says only that the probate code does not prevent a lien on estate property from being enforced; what counts as 'an appropriate proceeding' is for an attorney. Future-dated check: an existing registry note (pb-letters-required, 2026-11-12) records that the 2026 session's one PROBATE bill, S1240 (Ch. 79, effective 01/01/2027), replaces chapter 5 and amends 15-1-201 only; this section is not among them. That note was relied on, not re-run. The section page showed no effective-date banner on 2026-11-13.

claims.claim: Idaho Code 15-3-104 provides that no proceeding to enforce a claim against a decedent's estate may be commenced before a personal representative is appointed, and that the section has no application to a proceeding by a secured creditor of the decedent to enforce the creditor's right to the security, except as to any deficiency judgment that might be sought in it.
claims.quotedLanguage: No proceeding to enforce a claim against the estate of a decedent or his successors may be revived or commenced before the appointment of a personal representative. ... This section has no application to a proceeding by a secured creditor of the decedent to enforce his right to his security except as to any deficiency judgment which might be sought therein.
claims.notes: TRAP: describe, do not apply. The page says the statute separates a secured creditor's enforcement against its security from the estate-claims procedure, with deficiency judgments excepted. It must NOT say 'the lender can foreclose before probate is opened' as advice, and must not say whether an estate or heir owes a deficiency. Creditor-claim deadlines (15-3-803, existing claim pb-claims-barred-three-years) were not re-read for their effect on secured lenders. Future-dated check: an existing registry note (pb-letters-required, 2026-11-12) records that the 2026 session's one PROBATE bill, S1240 (Ch. 79, effective 01/01/2027), replaces chapter 5 and amends 15-1-201 only; this section is not among them. That note was relied on, not re-run. The section page showed no effective-date banner on 2026-11-13.

claims.claim: Under 24 CFR 206.27(c)(1), a HECM mortgage must state that the outstanding loan balance will be due and payable in full if a borrower dies and the property is not the principal residence of at least one surviving borrower, except that due and payable status is deferred if the requirements of the Deferral Period for an Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse are met.
claims.quotedLanguage: The mortgage shall state that the outstanding loan balance will be due and payable in full if a borrower dies and the property is not the principal residence of at least one surviving borrower, except that the due and payable status shall be deferred in accordance with paragraph (c)(3) of this section if the requirements of the Deferral Period are met
claims.notes: HECM (FHA-insured) only. The regulation prescribes what the mortgage must STATE; the loan documents themselves are the operative terms. Death is one trigger; 206.27(c)(2) lists others (moving out, unpaid property charges) that need the Commissioner's approval and are not this page's subject. Do not shorten to 'due when the borrower dies' without the surviving-borrower and deferral conditions.

claims.claim: 24 CFR 206.27(b)(8) requires a HECM mortgage to provide that the borrower has no personal liability for payment of the outstanding loan balance, that the mortgagee enforces the debt only through sale of the property, and that the mortgagee may not obtain a deficiency judgment against the borrower if the mortgage is foreclosed.
claims.quotedLanguage: The borrower shall have no personal liability for payment of the outstanding loan balance. The mortgagee shall enforce the debt only through sale of the property. The mortgagee shall not be permitted to obtain a deficiency judgment against the borrower if the mortgage is foreclosed.
claims.notes: HECM only. The text speaks of 'the borrower'. It does not mention heirs or the estate by name; the prose must quote it as written and must NOT say 'heirs can never owe anything'. The 'enforce the debt only through sale of the property' sentence is the supportable basis for describing the loan as non-recourse. Never extend to proprietary reverse mortgages.

claims.claim: 24 CFR 206.3 defines a HECM borrower as a mortgagor who is an original borrower under the HECM Loan Agreement and Note, and says the term does not include successors or assigns of a borrower; it defines a Non-Borrowing Spouse as the spouse of the HECM borrower at the time of closing who is not also a borrower.
claims.quotedLanguage: Borrower means a mortgagor who is an original borrower under the HECM Loan Agreement and Note. The term does not include successors or assigns of a borrower. ... Non-Borrowing Spouse means the spouse, as defined by the law of the state in which the spouse and borrower reside or the state of celebration, of the HECM borrower at the time of closing and who is also not a borrower.
claims.notes: Supports the plain statement that an heir who inherits the house is not a 'borrower' under part 206. Do not use it to decide who is or is not a borrower on a particular loan; the loan documents answer that.

claims.claim: 24 CFR 206.3 defines the Deferral Period as the period following the death of the last surviving borrower during which the due and payable status of a HECM is deferred for an Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse, provided the Qualifying Attributes and all other FHA requirements continue to be satisfied.
claims.quotedLanguage: Deferral Period means the period of time following the death of the last surviving borrower during which the due and payable status of a HECM is deferred for an Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse provided that the Qualifying Attributes and all other FHA requirements continue to be satisfied.
claims.notes: Definition only. The conditions are in 206.55 (rv-hecm-eligible-spouse-qualifying-attributes, rv-hecm-deferral-90-days-legal-right).

claims.claim: Under 24 CFR 206.125(a), the mortgagee must notify the FHA Commissioner within 60 days of a HECM becoming due and payable because of a death, must then notify the borrower's estate and heirs (and any Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse), as applicable, within 30 days that the mortgage is due and payable, and must give the applicable party 30 days from the date of that notice to take one of the listed actions.
claims.quotedLanguage: The mortgagee shall notify the Commissioner within 60 days of the mortgage becoming due and payable when the conditions stated in the mortgage, as required by § 206.27(c)(1) have occurred or when the Deferral Period ends. ... After notifying and receiving approval of the Commissioner when needed, the mortgagee shall notify the borrower, Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse, borrower's estate, and borrower's heir(s), as applicable, within 30 days of the later of notifying the Commissioner or receiving approval, if needed, that the mortgage is due and payable. The mortgagee shall give the applicable party 30 days from the date of notice to engage in the following actions:
claims.notes: HECM only. The 30 days to act run FROM THE DATE OF THE NOTICE, not from the death. The HUD 2019 fact sheet words this differently ('within 30 days of the date of the borrower's death'); see rv-hud-fact-sheet-30-days-and-90-day-extensions. State the regulation as the rule and flag the difference. These are duties placed on the mortgagee; never tell a reader how long they personally have.

claims.claim: The actions 24 CFR 206.125(a)(2) lists for the notified party include paying the outstanding loan balance in full, including accrued interest, mortgage insurance premium and mortgagee advances; selling the property; providing the mortgagee with a deed in lieu of foreclosure; and such other actions as the Commissioner permits through notice.
claims.quotedLanguage: Pay the outstanding loan balance, including any accrued interest, MIP, and mortgagee advances in full; ... Provide the mortgagee with a deed in lieu of foreclosure; ... Such other actions as permitted by the Commissioner through notice.
claims.notes: HECM only. Items (iv) and (v) (correcting a condition other than death; an Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse curing the end of a Deferral Period) are omitted because they do not apply to heirs after the last borrower's death. The sale option's price rule is in rv-hecm-sale-floor-95-percent-appraised. 'MIP' is mortgage insurance premium (206.27(b)(7) uses the term).

claims.claim: 24 CFR 206.125(a)(2)(ii) lets the notified party sell the property for an amount not less than the amount the Commissioner determines through notice, which may not exceed 95 percent of the appraised value, with the net proceeds applied to the outstanding loan balance; closing costs may not exceed the greater of 11 percent of the sales price or a fixed dollar amount set by the Commissioner; and for this section 'sell' includes the transfer of title by operation of law.
claims.quotedLanguage: Sell the property for an amount not to be less than the amount determined by the Commissioner through notice, which shall not exceed 95 percent of the appraised value as determined under § 206.125(b), with the net proceeds of the sale to be applied towards the outstanding loan balance. Closing costs shall not exceed the greater of: 11 percent of the sales price; or a fixed dollar amount as determined by the Commissioner through Federal Register notice. For the purposes of this section, sell includes the transfer of title by operation of law;
claims.notes: TRAP: the regulation does NOT itself say 'the lesser of the balance or 95 percent'. It says the minimum sale amount is set by the Commissioner through notice and that amount cannot exceed 95 percent of appraised value. The Commissioner's notice (a Mortgagee Letter or Federal Register notice) was NOT fetched, so the page must not state the current figure as fixed by the regulation; attribute '95 percent' as a floor to the CFPB and HUD pages. The appraised value is the 206.125(b) appraisal ordered by the mortgagee, not a listing price or a buyer's opinion. The fixed dollar closing-cost amount was not sourced; do not state one.

claims.claim: Under 24 CFR 206.125(b), the mortgagee must have the property appraised no later than 30 days after receiving a request from an applicable party in connection with a potential sale; when the mortgage is due and payable the appraisal is at the mortgagee's expense, but the mortgagee has a right to be reimbursed out of the proceeds of any sale.
claims.quotedLanguage: The mortgagee shall have the property appraised by an appraiser on the FHA roster, or other appraiser acceptable to, and identified by, the Commissioner through Federal Register notice, no later than 30 days after receipt of the request by an applicable party in connection with a potential property sale. ... If the mortgage is due and payable, the appraisal shall be at the mortgagee's expense but the mortgagee shall have a right to be reimbursed out of the proceeds of any sale by the borrower or other permissible party.
claims.notes: HECM only. This is the appraisal that the 95 percent figure is measured against. The business must never offer or promise an appraisal or a value.

claims.claim: Under 24 CFR 206.125(c), where a HECM is due and payable when the contract for sale is executed, the borrower or other party with legal right to dispose of the property may sell it in accordance with the amount established by 206.125(a)(2)(ii), and the mortgagee must satisfy the mortgage of record to facilitate the sale, provided there are no junior liens (other than a second mortgage to the Commissioner) and all the net proceeds from the sale are paid to the mortgagee.
claims.quotedLanguage: Where the HECM is due and payable at the time the contract for sale is executed, the borrower or other party with legal right to dispose of the property may sell the property in accordance with the amount established by § 206.125(a)(2)(ii). The mortgagee shall satisfy the mortgage of record (and the Commissioner will satisfy any second mortgage required by the Commissioner under § 206.27(d) of record) in order to facilitate the sale, provided that there are no junior liens (except the mortgage to secure payments by the Commissioner if required under § 206.27(d)) and all the net proceeds from the sale are paid to the mortgagee.
claims.notes: HECM only. Two conditions travel with the release: NO JUNIOR LIENS and ALL net proceeds to the mortgagee. Always state both. Who has 'legal right to dispose of the property' is a state-law question (Idaho probate claims pb-letters-required, pb-pr-may-sell-real-property). In a sale under this rule where the balance exceeds the price, nothing in this text sends money to the heirs.

claims.claim: 24 CFR 206.125(d) requires the mortgagee to commence foreclosure of a HECM within six months of the due date defined in 206.129(d)(1), or within such additional time as the Commissioner approves; if state or local law or federal bankruptcy law does not permit that, within six months after the prohibition expires.
claims.quotedLanguage: The mortgagee shall commence foreclosure of the mortgage within six months of the due date defined in § 206.129(d)(1), or within such additional time as may be approved by the Commissioner. ... the mortgagee shall commence foreclosure within six months after the expiration of the time during which such foreclosure is prohibited by such laws.
claims.notes: HECM only. This is a deadline on the MORTGAGEE to START foreclosure, with extensions in the Commissioner's discretion. It is not a guaranteed six months for heirs and must never be written as one. The start date is defined in rv-hecm-due-and-payable-date-definition. 206.125(d)(1) says 'due date'; 206.129(d)(1) defines 'Due and payable date'.

claims.claim: 24 CFR 206.129(d)(1) defines the due and payable date as the date the mortgagee notifies or should have notified the Commissioner that the mortgage is due and payable under the conditions required by 206.27(c)(1), or the date the Deferral Period ends, or the date the Commissioner approved a due and payable request.
claims.quotedLanguage: Due and payable date means the date when the mortgagee notifies or should have notified the Commissioner that the mortgage is due and payable under the conditions stated in the mortgage, as required by § 206.27(c)(1) or the date that the Deferral Period, as provided for in the mortgage by § 206.27(c)(3), ends; or the date the Commissioner approved a due and payable request as provided for in the mortgage by § 206.27(c)(2).
claims.notes: Only paragraph (d)(1) of 206.129 was used; the rest of the section is about insurance claim payments to the mortgagee. The date is tied to the mortgagee's notice to the Commissioner, which the heirs do not see. Do not convert it into a calendar date for a reader.

claims.claim: Under 24 CFR 206.125(f), the mortgagee must accept a deed in lieu of foreclosure from the borrower or other party with legal right to dispose of the property, provided it is filed for recording within 9 months of the due date and the mortgagee is able to obtain good and marketable title; in exchange the mortgagee cancels the credit instrument and satisfies the mortgage of record.
claims.quotedLanguage: the mortgagee shall accept a deed in lieu of foreclosure from the borrower or other party with legal right to dispose of the property provided it is filed for recording within 9 months of the due date and the mortgagee is able to obtain good and marketable title. ... In exchange for the executed and delivered deed, the mortgagee shall cancel the credit instrument and deliver it to the borrower and satisfy the mortgage of record.
claims.notes: HECM only. Conditional on GOOD AND MARKETABLE TITLE, which other liens or an unprobated estate can prevent. 206.125(f)(1)(ii) also mentions a possible 'Cash for Keys' incentive in an amount determined by the Commissioner; the amount and current availability were not sourced and it is left out of the page.

claims.claim: Under 24 CFR 206.55(a) and (c)(1), if the last surviving borrower dies before an Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse, due and payable status is deferred for as long as that spouse meets the Qualifying Attributes and the section's other requirements; to qualify the spouse must have been the borrower's spouse at loan closing and for the rest of the borrower's life, have been disclosed to the mortgagee at origination and specifically named as an Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse in the HECM documents, and have occupied and continue to occupy the property as a principal residence.
claims.quotedLanguage: If the last surviving borrower predeceases an Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse, and if the requirements of paragraph (d) of this section are satisfied, the due and payable status will be deferred for as long as the Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse continues to meet the Qualifying Attributes in paragraph (c) of this section and the requirements of paragraphs (d) and (e) of this section. ... Have been the spouse of a HECM borrower at the time of loan closing and remained the spouse of such HECM borrower for the duration of the HECM borrower's lifetime; ... Have been properly disclosed to the mortgagee at origination and specifically named as an Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse in the HECM mortgage and loan documents; ... Have occupied, and continue to occupy, the property securing the HECM as his or her principal residence; and
claims.notes: HECM only. 206.55(c)(1)(iv) adds 'any other requirements as the Commissioner may prescribe'; say the list is not exhaustive. This is the CURRENT regulation; the CFPB says older loans (FHA case numbers before August 4, 2014) follow a different process (rv-cfpb-nonborrowing-spouse-case-number-date). Never tell a spouse whether they qualify.

claims.claim: 24 CFR 206.55(d) requires an Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse, within 90 days from the death of the last surviving HECM borrower, to establish legal ownership or another ongoing legal right to remain for life in the property, and afterwards to ensure the borrower's other loan obligations continue to be satisfied; 206.55(f) says nothing in the section interferes with the ability of the borrower's estate or heirs to dispose of the property if they are otherwise legally entitled to do so.
claims.quotedLanguage: Within 90 days from the death of the last surviving HECM borrower, establish legal ownership or other ongoing legal right to remain for life in the property securing the HECM; ... After the death of the last surviving borrower, ensure all other obligations of the HECM borrower(s) contained in the loan documents continue to be satisfied; and ... Nothing in this section may be construed as interrupting or interfering with the ability of the borrower's estate or heir(s) to dispose of the property if they are otherwise legally entitled to do so.
claims.notes: HECM only. The 90 days here runs from the DEATH and applies to the surviving spouse, not to heirs generally. How a spouse establishes ownership in Idaho (community property, probate, survivorship) is an attorney question and is not addressed.

claims.claim: Under 24 CFR 206.55(b)(1) and (c)(2), if a Non-Borrowing Spouse no longer satisfies the Qualifying Attributes, the mortgagee may not provide an opportunity to cure and the HECM becomes immediately due and payable as a result of the death of the last surviving borrower; a spouse who was ineligible for the Deferral Period at loan origination does not become eligible later when the borrowing spouse dies.
claims.quotedLanguage: If a Deferral Period ceases or becomes unavailable because a Non-Borrowing Spouse no longer satisfies the Qualifying Attributes and has become an Ineligible Non-Borrowing Spouse, a mortgagee may not provide an opportunity to cure the default, and the HECM will become immediately due and payable as a result of the death of the last surviving borrower. ... A Non-Borrowing Spouse that is ineligible for the Deferral Period at the time of loan origination because he or she failed to satisfy the Qualifying Attributes requirements in paragraph (c)(1) of this section is not subsequently eligible for a Deferral Period when the borrowing spouse dies or moves out of the home.
claims.notes: HECM only. Keep attributed and general. 206.55(b)(2) and 206.57 give a 30-day cure where the spouse still meets the attributes; 206.57 was not read in full and the cure is not described on the page.

claims.claim: The CFPB says a reverse mortgage loan becomes due and payable after the borrower's death and the death of any coborrowers or eligible nonborrowing spouse; that once heirs receive a due and payable notice from the lender they have 30 days to buy, sell, or turn the home over to the lender; that this is the case for HECMs; and that it might be possible for the timeline to be extended up to six months so heirs can sell the home or obtain their own loan.
claims.quotedLanguage: A reverse mortgage loan becomes due and payable after your death and after the death of any coborrowers or of an eligible nonborrowing spouse. Once your heirs receive a due and payable notice from the lender, they have 30 days to buy, sell, or turn the home over to the lender to satisfy the debt. This is the case for Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs), which are the most common type of reverse mortgage loan. ... However, it might be possible for the timeline to be extended up to six months so your heirs can sell the home or obtain their own loan to purchase the home. Your heirs can consult a HUD-approved housing counseling agency or an attorney for more information.
claims.notes: Page last reviewed AUG 28, 2026. 'MIGHT be possible ... UP TO six months' is the CFPB's wording; keep both hedges. The CFPB does not say who grants the extension or on what showing. Never write 'heirs get six months'. CFPB disclaimer: general consumer information, not legal advice or regulatory guidance.

claims.claim: The CFPB says that where there is no coborrower or eligible nonborrowing spouse, heirs who want to keep the home must pay the full loan balance, and to sell it they must repay the full loan balance, or at least 95 percent of its appraised value if the loan balance owed is more than the home value.
claims.quotedLanguage: It depends on whether there are coborrowers or an eligible nonborrowing spouse. If there are neither, to keep the home, heirs must pay the full loan balance. To sell it, they must repay the full loan balance, or at least 95 percent of its appraised value if the loan balance owed is more than the home value.
claims.notes: Page last reviewed AUG 28, 2026; applies to HECMs per the same page. CONFLICT TO CARRY: this newer page says keeping the home takes the FULL balance; the older CFPB page (rv-cfpb-heirs-lesser-of-balance-or-95-percent, reviewed JAN 02, 2025) says heirs who want to keep the home repay the lesser of the balance or 95 percent. The page states both, dated, and does not resolve them.

claims.claim: The CFPB says that when the home is worth more than the amount owed on the reverse mortgage, heirs can sell the home, repay the loan and keep the difference; and that when the home is worth less than the amount owed, heirs can pay off the loan by selling the home for at least 95 percent of its appraised value, with the rest of the loan covered by the mortgage insurance the borrower paid during the loan.
claims.quotedLanguage: your home might be worth more than the amount owed on the reverse mortgage. This means your heirs can sell the home, use the money to repay the loan, and keep the difference. ... your home might be worth less than the amount owed on the reverse mortgage. This means your heirs can pay off the loan by selling the home for at least 95 percent of the home's appraised value. The rest of the loan is covered by the mortgage insurance that the reverse mortgage borrower paid during the duration of the loan.
claims.notes: Page last reviewed AUG 28, 2026; HECM only (mortgage insurance is the FHA insurance). 'Keep the difference' is before sale costs, other liens and estate debts; do not promise a net figure.

claims.claim: A CFPB page last reviewed January 2, 2025 says that heirs who want to keep the home after the borrower and any Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse die will have to repay either the full loan balance or 95 percent of the home's appraised value, whichever is less.
claims.quotedLanguage: If your heirs want to keep your home after you and your Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse die, your heirs will have to repay either the full loan balance or 95 percent of the home's appraised value – whichever is less.
claims.notes: MEDIUM: the CFPB's own newer page (reviewed AUG 28, 2026) says keeping the home requires the full balance, and HUD's 2019 fact sheet says the same. The regulation supports a reading under which a transfer to an heir counts as a sale ('sell includes the transfer of title by operation of law'), but it does not state a lesser-of rule in terms. State this claim ONLY with its date and next to the conflicting sources.

claims.claim: The CFPB says that when there is a co-borrower on a reverse mortgage and one borrower dies, the co-borrower will be able to remain in the home and receive loan payments as long as they meet the obligations of the loan.
claims.quotedLanguage: If one borrower dies, the co-borrower will be able to remain in the home and receive loan payments as long as they meet the obligations of the reverse mortgage loan
claims.notes: Page last reviewed JAN 02, 2025. Consistent with 206.27(c)(1) (rv-hecm-due-when-last-borrower-dies).

claims.claim: The CFPB says a non-borrowing spouse may be able to stay in the home without paying off the loan, depending on when the loan was taken out and whether they qualify as an Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse under HUD rules; that an Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse will not get any money from the reverse mortgage; that qualifying may be difficult; and it describes separate processes for HECMs with FHA case numbers assigned on or after August 4, 2014 and before that date.
claims.quotedLanguage: They may also be able to stay in the home without paying off the loan, depending on when the loan was taken out and whether they qualify as an Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse under U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) rules. An Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse will not get any money from the reverse mortgage. The process of qualifying to be an Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse may be difficult. ... For HECMs with Federal Housing Administration (FHA) case numbers assigned on or after August 4, 2014 ... For HECMs with FHA case numbers assigned before August 4, 2014
claims.notes: Page last reviewed JAN 02, 2025. The pre-August 2014 process (Mortgagee Optional Election assignment, which the lender may choose) is described by the CFPB but its HUD source (Mortgagee Letters) was not fetched; the page only says the process differs and points to the servicer, a counselor or an attorney.

claims.claim: The CFPB says there are several kinds of reverse mortgage loans: those insured by the Federal Housing Administration, proprietary reverse mortgage loans that are not FHA-insured, and single-purpose reverse mortgage loans offered by state and local governments; that most reverse mortgage loans today are HECMs insured by the FHA; and that non-HECM reverse mortgage loans are not federally insured.
claims.quotedLanguage: There are several kinds of reverse mortgage loans: (1) those insured by the Federal Housing Administration (FHA); (2) proprietary reverse mortgage loans that are not FHA-insured; and (3) single-purpose reverse mortgage loans offered by state and local governments. ... Most reverse mortgage loans today are Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs), insured by the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), which is a part of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). ... These non-HECM reverse mortgage loans are not federally insured.
claims.notes: Page last reviewed JUL 11, 2022 (oldest CFPB page used). Basis for limiting every rule on the page to HECMs. Nothing was sourced about what proprietary loan documents say at death; the page says only that their own documents control.

claims.claim: The CFPB says that with a reverse mortgage loan the title to the home remains in the borrower's name, borrowers do not make monthly mortgage payments, interest and fees are added to the loan balance each month so the balance grows, and the homeowners or their heirs will eventually have to pay back the loan, usually by selling the home.
claims.quotedLanguage: when you take out a reverse mortgage loan, the title to your home remains in your name. However, unlike a traditional mortgage, with a reverse mortgage loan, borrowers don't make monthly mortgage payments. ... Interest and fees are added to the loan balance each month and the balance grows. ... The homeowners or their heirs will eventually have to pay back the loan, usually by selling the home.
claims.notes: Page last reviewed AUG 28, 2026; the page says its information applies only to HECMs.

claims.claim: HUD says the only reverse mortgage insured by the U.S. Federal Government is the Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM), which is available only through an FHA-approved lender.
claims.quotedLanguage: The only reverse mortgage insured by the U.S. Federal Government is called a Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM), and is only available through a Federal Housing Administration (FHA)-approved lender.
claims.notes: MEDIUM because the HUD page carries no visible date. Pairs with rv-cfpb-three-types-of-reverse-mortgage.

claims.claim: HUD's fact sheet on inheriting a home secured by an FHA-insured HECM (dated 9/2019) says that if the loan balance is more than the home is worth, the estate or heirs may sell the home for at least 95 percent of the current appraised value and the lender will accept the net proceeds as satisfaction of the loan, that any post-death transfer is considered a 'sale' for these purposes, and that heirs who prefer to keep the home must pay off the HECM loan balance in full.
claims.quotedLanguage: If the loan balance is more than the home is worth, the estate or heirs may sell the home for at least 95-percent of the current appraised value and the lender will accept the net proceeds as satisfaction of the loan. Any post death transfer is considered a "sale" for these purposes. ... If you prefer to keep the home instead of selling it, the HECM loan balance must be paid off in full.
claims.notes: MEDIUM: one-page consumer fact sheet dated 9/2019, still linked from HUD's current HECM page on 2026-11-13. It contains both 'any post death transfer is considered a sale' and 'keeping the home ... paid off in full', which is the same tension as between the two CFPB pages. Quote it, date it, do not resolve it. The fact sheet's 'Know Your Options' sentence is garbled in the PDF ('estate or heirs (other than a non-borrowing spouse*) HECM loan or transfer title') and is not quoted.

claims.claim: HUD's 9/2019 fact sheet says the loan must be satisfied within 30 days of the date of the borrower's death, and that the lender may approve 90-day extensions with satisfactory documentation that the estate or heirs are actively trying to sell the property or repay the HECM loan.
claims.quotedLanguage: The loan must be satisfied within 30 days of the date of the borrower's death. ... The lender may approve 90-day extensions with satisfactory documentation ... that the estate or heirs are actively trying to sell the property or repay the
claims.notes: MEDIUM. CONFLICT: the fact sheet counts 30 days from the DEATH; 24 CFR 206.125(a)(2) counts 30 days from the DATE OF THE NOTICE and the CFPB (2026) says the same. The regulation controls; the page states the difference. The fact sheet does not say how many 90-day extensions exist; do not write 'two extensions' or 'up to a year'. Extensions are discretionary ('may approve'). The quote is joined with ellipses because the two-column PDF interleaves sidebar text between the lines in the extracted text; the passage is continuous in the original, ending 'repay the HECM loan.'

claims.claim: HUD's 9/2019 fact sheet says property taxes and insurance on the property remain the responsibility of the borrower's estate until title is transferred, and tells heirs to contact the HECM lender immediately to review their responsibilities and options.
claims.quotedLanguage: Property taxes and insurance on the property remain the responsibility of the borrower's estate until title is transferred. ... Contact the HECM lender immediately to review your responsibilities and options.
claims.notes: MEDIUM (2019 fact sheet). Pairs with the existing Idaho claim pb-pr-possession-and-taxes.

claims.claim: IRS Topic 701 says a taxpayer with a capital gain from the sale of a main home may qualify to exclude up to $250,000 of that gain from income, or up to $500,000 on a joint return with a spouse.
claims.quotedLanguage: If you have a capital gain from the sale of your main home, you may qualify to exclude up to $250,000 of that gain from your income, or up to $500,000 of that gain if you file a joint return with your spouse.
claims.notes: 'May qualify', and only for a MAIN home. Topic 701 reads 'Page Last Reviewed or Updated: 09-Nov-2026' and gives no tax year for the figures. Never write that a seller 'will not owe tax'. Always pair with the ownership and use tests.

claims.claim: IRS Topic 701 says that in general a seller must meet both an ownership test and a use test: owning the home for at least 24 months out of the 5 years leading up to the sale, and using it as a residence for at least 24 months of the previous 5 years. The two tests can be met during different 2-year periods, but both must be met within the 5-year period ending on the date of sale.
claims.quotedLanguage: In general, to qualify for this exclusion, you must meet both the ownership test and the use test. ... owned the home for at least 24 months (2 years) out of the last 5 years leading up to the date of the sale, you meet the ownership test. ... used the home as a residence for at least 24 months (2 years) of the previous 5 years, you meet the use test. You can meet the ownership and use tests during different 2-year periods. However, you must meet both tests during the 5-year period ending on the date of the sale.
claims.notes: 'In general'. Publication 523 holds exceptions (surviving spouses, military, partial exclusion). Do not tell a reader whether they pass the tests.

claims.claim: IRS Topic 701 says a seller is generally not eligible for the exclusion if they excluded the gain from the sale of another home during the two-year period before the sale.
claims.quotedLanguage: not eligible for the exclusion if you excluded the gain from the sale of another home during the two-year period prior to the sale of your home.
claims.notes: 'Generally'. Topic 701 refers to Publication 523 for exceptions to the two-year rule.

claims.claim: IRS Topic 701 says a seller who receives an informational document such as Form 1099-S must report the sale of the home even if the gain is excludable, and must also report the sale if not all of the gain can be excluded; Schedule D (Form 1040) and Form 8949 are used when the sale must be reported.
claims.quotedLanguage: you must report the sale of the home even if the gain from the sale is excludable. Additionally, you must report the sale of the home if you can't exclude all of your capital gain from income. Use Schedule D (Form 1040), Capital Gains and Losses and Form 8949, Sales and Other Dispositions of Capital Assets when required to report the home sale.
claims.notes: Reporting is not the same as owing tax. Pair with cl-1099s-principal-residence-certification, which is about whether the closing agent files the form at all.

claims.claim: IRS Publication 523 (2025) says that for a married couple filing jointly only one spouse has to meet the ownership requirement, that the residence requirement is a total of 24 months (730 days) within the 5-year period and need not be one block of time, and that each spouse must meet the residence requirement individually for the couple to get the full exclusion.
claims.quotedLanguage: For a married couple filing jointly, only one spouse has to meet the ownership requirement. ... The 24 months of residence can fall anywhere within the 5-year period, and it doesn't have to be a single block of time. All that is required is a total of 24 months (730 days) of residence during the 5-year period. Unlike the ownership requirement, each spouse must meet the residence requirement individually for a married couple filing jointly to get the full exclusion.
claims.notes: Publication 523 is the 2025 edition ('For use in preparing 2025 Returns'; page last reviewed 30-Apr-2026). No 2026 edition existed on 2026-11-13. State the edition year in prose.

claims.claim: IRS Publication 523 (2025) says a seller who does not meet the Eligibility Test may still qualify for a partial exclusion of gain if the main reason for the home sale was a change in workplace location, a health issue, or an unforeseeable event.
claims.quotedLanguage: If you don't meet the Eligibility Test, you may still qualify for a partial exclusion of gain. You can meet the requirements for a partial exclusion if the main reason for your home sale was a change in workplace location, a health issue, or an unforeseeable event.
claims.notes: Publication 523 defines each of these events in detail. Do NOT say that financial hardship or foreclosure counts; the detailed lists were not claimed. Describe and point to the publication and a tax professional.

claims.claim: IRS Publication 523 (2025) says that to figure gain or loss on the sale of a main home a seller must know the selling price, the amount realized and the adjusted basis, and subtracts the adjusted basis from the amount realized; the worksheet describes the amount realized as the sale price minus selling expenses.
claims.quotedLanguage: To figure the gain or loss on the sale of your main home, you must know the selling price, the amount realized, and the adjusted basis. Subtract the adjusted basis from the amount realized to get your gain or loss. ... (sale price minus selling expenses)
claims.notes: Gain is NOT the cash a seller walks away with and is NOT sale price minus mortgage payoff. The prose may say the mortgage balance does not appear in the IRS formula only because the formula quoted has three terms; do not go further.

claims.claim: IRS Publication 523 (2025) says that when the adjusted basis is greater than the amount realized the home was sold at a loss, that the loss cannot be deducted, and that no tax is due on the money received from the sale.
claims.quotedLanguage: If the number is negative (adjusted basis is greater than amount realized), you sold your home at a loss. You can't deduct this loss, but you don't need to pay any tax on the money you received from selling your home.
claims.notes: This is the main-home worksheet. It does not describe a rental or investment property, and it does not address canceled debt (see ss-irs-* claims).

claims.claim: IRS Publication 523 (2025) says gain from the sale of a main home is not excludable to the extent it is allocable to periods of nonqualified use, meaning any period after 2008 when neither the seller nor the seller's spouse or former spouse used the property as a main home, with certain exceptions.
claims.quotedLanguage: Gain from the sale or exchange of your main home isn't excludable from income if it is allocable to periods of nonqualified use. Nonqualified use means any period after 2008 when neither you nor your spouse (or former spouse) used the property as your main home, with certain exceptions.
claims.notes: 'With certain exceptions': the publication lists them (for example time after the last use as a main home within the 5-year period). The exceptions were NOT claimed; say they exist and stop.

claims.claim: IRS Publication 523 (2025) says a seller who was entitled to take depreciation deductions because the home was used for business or as rental property cannot exclude the part of the gain equal to any depreciation allowed or allowable for periods after May 6, 1997.
claims.quotedLanguage: If you were entitled to take depreciation deductions because you used your home for business purposes or as rental property, you cannot exclude the part of your gain equal to any depreciation allowed or allowable as a deduction for periods after May 6, 1997.
claims.notes: 'Allowed or allowable' means depreciation counts whether or not it was actually claimed. Recapture mechanics (Form 4797, Pub 544) were not claimed.

claims.claim: IRS Publication 523 (2025) says the basis of a home inherited from a decedent is the fair market value of the property on the date of the decedent's death, or on the later alternate valuation date chosen by the personal representative of the estate, and that if a federal estate tax return (Form 706) was filed or required, the value listed on that return is the basis.
claims.quotedLanguage: If you inherited your home from a decedent who died before or after 2010, your basis is the fair market value of the property on the date of the decedent's death (or the later alternate valuation date chosen by the personal representative of the estate). If a federal estate tax return (Form 706) was filed or required to be filed, the value of the property listed on the estate tax return is your basis.
claims.notes: The IRS never uses the phrase 'stepped-up basis' in the passages quoted; the prose may say the rule is commonly called that only as a label, and must give the IRS wording. The value can be lower than the decedent's cost as well as higher. Do not say an heir 'owes no tax'.

claims.claim: IRS Publication 551 (revised December 2025) says the basis of property inherited from a decedent is generally the fair market value of the property at the date of the individual's death, or the fair market value on the alternate valuation date if the personal representative chooses alternate valuation, among other listed possibilities.
claims.quotedLanguage: Generally, the basis of property inherited from a decedent is one of the following. ... The FMV of the property at the date of the individual's death. ... The FMV on the alternate valuation date if the personal representative for the estate chooses to use alternate valuation.
claims.notes: 'Generally' and 'one of the following': the list also has special-use valuation and a conservation-easement case, and the publication has a one-year gift-back exception for appreciated property. Where Form 706 was required, a consistent-basis rule and Schedule A (Form 8971) apply. None of that is applied to a reader.

claims.claim: IRS Publication 551 (revised December 2025) lists Idaho among the community property states and says that when either spouse dies, the total value of the community property, even the part belonging to the surviving spouse, generally becomes the basis of the entire property, provided at least half the value of the community property interest is includible in the decedent's gross estate.
claims.quotedLanguage: In community property states (Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin), married individuals are each usually considered to own half the community property. When either spouse dies, the total value of the community property, even the part belonging to the surviving spouse, generally becomes the basis of the entire property. For this rule to apply, at least half the value of the community property interest must be includible in the decedent's gross estate, whether or not the estate must file a return.
claims.notes: Applies to COMMUNITY property. Whether a particular Idaho house was community or separate property is an Idaho law question the page must not answer. 'Generally' and 'usually' must survive into prose.

claims.claim: IRS Topic 703 says the basis of an asset is in most situations its cost, that a taxpayer must determine adjusted basis before figuring gain or loss on a sale, and that basis is increased by items such as the cost of improvements that add to the value of the property and decreased by items such as allowable depreciation and insurance reimbursements for casualty and theft losses.
claims.quotedLanguage: In most situations, the basis of an asset is its cost to you. ... Before figuring gain or loss on a sale, exchange, or other disposition of property, or before figuring allowable depreciation, you must determine your adjusted basis in that property. ... Increase your basis by items such as the cost of improvements that add to the value of the property, and decrease it by items such as allowable depreciation and insurance reimbursements for casualty and theft losses.
claims.notes: Topic 703 reads 'Page Last Reviewed or Updated: 09-Nov-2026'. Which costs count as improvements rather than repairs is in Publication 523 and was not claimed; do not list examples.

claims.claim: IRS Topic 409 says a capital gain or loss is generally long-term if the asset was held for more than one year before disposal and short-term if held one year or less, with exceptions that include property acquired from a decedent, and that net short-term capital gains are taxed as ordinary income at graduated rates.
claims.quotedLanguage: Generally, if you hold the asset for more than one year before you dispose of it, your capital gain or loss is long-term. If you hold it one year or less, your capital gain or loss is short-term. For exceptions to this rule, such as property acquired by gift, property acquired from a decedent, or patent property, refer to Publication 544 ... Net short-term capital gains are subject to taxation as ordinary income at graduated tax rates.
claims.notes: The decedent exception itself is in Publication 544, which was NOT read. The page may say an exception exists for property acquired from a decedent; it must not say what the exception is.

claims.claim: IRS Topic 409, last reviewed 9 November 2026, says that for taxable years beginning in 2025 the tax rate on most net capital gain is no higher than 15% for most individuals, that some or all net capital gain may be taxed at 0%, that a 20% rate applies to the extent taxable income exceeds the thresholds set for the 15% rate, and that the portion of any unrecaptured section 1250 gain from selling section 1250 real property is taxed at a maximum 25% rate.
claims.quotedLanguage: Net capital gains are taxed at different rates depending on overall taxable income, although some or all net capital gain may be taxed at 0% ... For taxable years beginning in 2025, the tax rate on most net capital gain is no higher than 15% for most individuals. ... However, a capital gains rate of 20% applies to the extent that your taxable income exceeds the thresholds set for the 15% capital gain rate. ... The portion of any unrecaptured section 1250 gain from selling section 1250 real property is taxed at a maximum 25% rate.
claims.notes: TAX YEAR 2025 figures, on a page reviewed in November 2026. The page did not give thresholds for taxable years beginning in 2026, and the income thresholds are indexed, so the dollar thresholds are deliberately NOT claimed. Always write 'for taxable years beginning in 2025'. Topic 409 also mentions the net investment income tax (Topic 559), which was not read. MEDIUM only because a 2026 sale is a 2026-tax-year event and the page speaks to 2025.

claims.claim: Idaho Code 63-3011B defines 'taxable income' as federal taxable income as determined under the Internal Revenue Code, and 63-3011C defines 'Idaho taxable income' as taxable income as modified by the Idaho adjustments specifically provided in the income tax chapter.
claims.quotedLanguage: The term "taxable income" means federal taxable income as determined under the Internal Revenue Code. ... The term "Idaho taxable income" means taxable income as modified pursuant to the Idaho adjustments specifically provided in this chapter.
claims.notes: Two sections, one sentence each. amendmentHistory holds 63-3011B's note; 63-3011C's note reads '[63-3011C, added 1995, ch. 111, sec. 5, p. 350.]' (verified on the cached page). This supports ONLY the statement that Idaho's computation starts from federal taxable income. It does NOT by itself prove that every federal exclusion carries into Idaho for every taxpayer; which version of the Internal Revenue Code Idaho conforms to (63-3004) was not read. Keep the prose to the definitions.

claims.claim: Idaho Code 63-3022H(1) gives an individual taxpayer who reports capital gain net income in determining Idaho taxable income a deduction of sixty percent of the capital gain net income from the sale or exchange of qualified property (eighty percent applied only to taxable year 2001).
claims.quotedLanguage: If an individual taxpayer reports capital gain net income in determining Idaho taxable income, eighty percent (80%) in taxable year 2001 and sixty percent (60%) in taxable years thereafter of the capital gain net income from the sale or exchange of qualified property shall be a deduction in determining Idaho taxable income.
claims.notes: A DEDUCTION of 60% of qualifying gain, not a 60% tax rate and not a 60% cut in tax. INDIVIDUAL taxpayers. Only 'qualified property'. Always state with the limits in subsection (2).

claims.claim: Under Idaho Code 63-3022H(3), property held by an estate, trust, S corporation, partnership, limited liability company or an individual is qualified property if it had an Idaho situs at the time of sale and is, among other listed categories, real property held at least twelve months.
claims.quotedLanguage: Property held by an estate, trust, S corporation, partnership, limited liability company or an individual is "qualified property" under this section if the property had an Idaho situs at the time of sale and is: ... (a) Real property held at least twelve (12) months;
claims.notes: The other categories (business tangible personal property, livestock, timber, certain partnership interests) are irrelevant to a house and are not described. Holding period is counted under subsection (4) by reference to Internal Revenue Code section 1223; how that treats inherited property was NOT sourced.

claims.claim: Idaho Code 63-3022H(6) says that, as used in the section, 'real property' means land and includes a qualified conservation easement, certain grazing permits or leases, and any other property defined in section 1250(c) of the Internal Revenue Code as 'section 1250 property' conveyed in perpetuity whose transfer must be in writing under Idaho Code 9-503. Subsection (7) excludes property depreciated under section 1245 of the Internal Revenue Code.
claims.quotedLanguage: As used in this section, the term "real property" means land and includes the following: ... (c) Any other property defined in section 1250(c) of the Internal Revenue Code as "section 1250 property" conveyed in perpetuity, the transfer of which would be required to be in writing by section 9-503, Idaho Code. ... Property that has been depreciated pursuant to section 1245 of the Internal Revenue Code is not eligible to be treated as real property for purposes of this deduction.
claims.notes: THE TRAP. The statute does NOT use the words house, home, dwelling or residence anywhere. It says 'land' plus 'section 1250 property', a federal term that was not read (26 U.S.C. 1250(c) was not fetched; the Tax Commission's Form CG instructions paraphrase it as 'depreciable real property'). The page must say the statute names land and section 1250 property and does not name a house, then report what the Tax Commission's form does (cg-istc-form-cg-2025-residence-line). Never write 'Idaho Code 63-3022H covers your house'.

claims.claim: Idaho Code 63-3022H(2) limits the deduction to the amount of capital gain net income from all property included in taxable income, excludes gains treated as ordinary income by the Internal Revenue Code, and reduces the deduction by any federal capital gains deduction relating to the property.
